idiom_name: java.util.stream Stream.filter/map chain with a terminal collect/reduce
implementation_notes: The JDK's realisation: a Stream is a lazily-evaluated pipeline over any source (collections, arrays, I/O, Stream.iterate/generate), intermediate operations (filter/map/flatMap/distinct/sorted/limit) compose by chaining, and a terminal operation both drives the pipeline and supplies the sink - the reduction half is factored into a Collector (supplier/accumulator/combiner/finisher) or the three-argument Stream.reduce. What replaces the classic structure: the reducing function is a Collector object and the transformation stack is the stream chain; the classic transducer is only needed when a custom intermediate operation must be defined once and reused across chains (Java 24 gatherers) or when the destination is not a stream consumer. The single-use stream and the mandatory terminal are the price of the design and the reason a stream reference cannot be treated as a stored pipeline.
code_sketch:
List<String> ids = readings.stream()
    .filter(Reading::isValid)
    .map(r -> r.sensor() + ":" + r.value())
    .limit(100)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());              // terminal drives the pipeline
// custom reduction (the 'job'): Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher)
long n = readings.stream().filter(Reading::isValid).count();   // a different sink, same stages
pitfalls: A Stream is single-use: reusing a stream reference (or any intermediate stream) throws IllegalStateException - keep the source (collection or Supplier) and rebuild the pipeline per traversal.
A Collector used with a parallel stream must satisfy identity and associativity and provide a real combiner; a stateful or non-associative collector silently produces wrong results under parallel().
peek and lambda side effects are not a debugging contract: elements can be skipped under short-circuiting and are evaluated in an unspecified order under parallel streams.

variants.name: Stream Gatherer (Java 24)
variants.implementation_notes: JEP 485 adds custom intermediate operations to the Stream API: a Gatherer<T,A,R> is defined by four cooperating functions - initializer (private state), integrator (element in, possibly several elements out, and a boolean return that stops the stream), optional combiner (parallel evaluation) and optional finisher (end-of-stream, e.g. flush a buffer) - and Stream.gather applies it exactly like a built-in intermediate operation. This is the transducer protocol in Java form: the integrator is the step, the finisher is the completion arity, the combiner is the parallel merge, and gatherers compose with andThen just as transducers compose with comp. Choose it over a plain stream chain when the transformation (windowing, dedupe-by, custom scan) cannot be expressed with built-ins without materialising intermediates, or when an infinite stream must short-circuit; the Gatherers factory class already ships fold, scan, windowFixed, windowSliding and mapConcurrent. Code that must run below Java 24 has no equivalent and has to hand-roll the operation over a Spliterator.
pitfalls: Gatherer state is per-partition, never shared: it must not escape to other threads, and a gatherer without a combiner silently falls back to sequential evaluation inside a parallel stream.

The integrator's boolean return is the only short-circuit signal; returning true forever means an infinite upstream never ends, and a missing finisher loses the last partial window of a buffering stage.
Gatherers are new API surface (Java 24): libraries targeting older runtimes must fall back to Stream chains or a custom Spliterator, and the two realisations do not compose across that boundary.
